utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic. I notice the absence of Mr. Milutinovic who is unwell but the proceedings will proceed in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note that Mr. Milutinovic is not with us, and I gather he's unwell but content that we should continue with the trial in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mitic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning continues to apply to your evidence until it is completed. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. We left off yesterday just starting to look at the document 6D140 which I would ask to be brought up on e-court again. This was the order from the command of the military district in Pristina, your superior, dated the 27th of March, 1999. And when we get to that document, I will ask for the fourth page of the same to be brought up, I believe both in the B/C/S and the English. That's item number 7, specifically I take it it's going to be the -- the fifth page is the part I want to -- to look at that and ask if indeed section 7.1, 7.2, and 7.3 -- it should be 6D1470. That's the document. If you could turn to --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can we please zoom in a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if we --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 on this page can you confirm for me that this document, this order, provides concrete assignments for the military territorial detachment units in your zone, that is to say in Prizren, Orahovac, and Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the command of the Pristina military district. It contains tasks, but as a plan and not as an order that must be executed. It comprises all military districts -- or, rather, military recruitment offices in the Pristina military district. We have the Pristina one, the Kosovska Mitrovica one, the Pec one, the Gnjilane one, and of course the Prizren military recruitment office, and the tasks are listed for all of these detachments and for the command with all its component units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these tasks -- first of all, do you recall receiving this -- this document from your superior officer around March 27th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order came, and it was filed. The portion that pertains to me was, in practical terms, a task for my plan, my future plan, which was then subsequently approved by the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And just so there's no confusion, do you recall that the tasks that were included in this order from the military district in Pristina specifically for your units at the military department in Prizren included securing important locations, protecting the civilian population in the cities and towns of Prizren, Suva Reka, Orahovac, and some nearby villages, and combat control of terrain on the line Prizren-Suva Reka, Suva Reka-Dulje, Orahovac-Zrze among others and also securing of roadways? Do you recall receiving those tasks for your units from your superior officers in the military territorial district in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again these are general tasks that were planned for future actions, but every time there is a combat operation a special order is drafted for each and every one of those. Therefore some of these detachments may be resubordinated to a different unit and then the commander will shall issuing orders to that unit. These were the tasks that were -- were being planned at the time. This is the planning stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we move along to actual tasks undertaken, would you agree with me that the military territorial detachment units in your zone of Prizren, both on their own and in coordination with units of the Pristina Corps and the Ministry of Interior carried out legitimate anti-terrorist actions in 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on the military territorial detachment and on the deployment of the 549th Brigade and the 242nd Armoured Brigade. The commander issued me orders to attach certain units to those units. As for all the other units, I exercised command depending on the situation and in coordination with the commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade. Occasionally, I was also informed about other forces that perhaps happened to be somewhere nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. To just clarify that -- let me do it this way. This might be easier for you: If we look very briefly at Exhibit 5D30. And, sir, I'll draw your attention to paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 of this document once it comes up on the screen. First of all, it's -- it's a report of the military territorial district in Pristina, and I believe that paragraphs 2, 3, and 4 of this document discuss coordinated combat undertaken by your units or units from your zone alongside the MUP and the Pristina Corps in the region of Lusta Klina, et cetera. Do you recall that your forces did indeed participate alongside both the Ministry of Interior and VJ forces in a legitimate anti-terrorist action, and the date of the document if we can scroll up, I think it was around the 1st of June is what my notes say. Do you recall the forces, units from your zone participating in this action?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see immediately under item 2 that these are not my units. Therefore -- can we please move the page down a little to one of the next items. 180, that detachment is not mine. From it's from Kosovska Mitrovica. Move on, please. Then we see Gnjilane. Not mine. Move on. Pristina, not mine either. And there's nothing left, is there? This document is not mine. It's not in reference to me. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with either your units or other military territorial detachments from other zones undertaking independent anti -- legitimate anti-terrorist actions during 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military recruitment offices were not set up for operations such as these. If there is joint action with another unit he must receive specific assignments from the commander of that unit, but the military territorial detachment was mostly to be used to exercise control along the depth of the territory to secure certain roads, to guard certain vital facilities but not for anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say the military recruitment offices were not set up for operations such as these. I'd like to turn your attention to 5D1074. And as we wait for that document, we will see that it's also a combat report from the command of the military district in Pristina, and if we look at the first two paragraphs of this report from Colonel Pesic, your superior, he seems to be talking about the 115th and the 174th military territorial detachment units undertaking an action, doing their own blockade and doing their own smashing of terrorist forces in Veliki, Belacevac, Gospodja [phoen], Sisan, Donji Grabovac. Will this refresh your recollection as to whether or not if perhaps not in your zone, in other zones the military territorial recruitment offices did undertake legitimate anti-terrorist actions on their own initiative, that they were in fact set up and authorised or capable of doing so?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. These are not my units. In my area of responsibility there were no situations like these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, let's move to something this witness knows about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. That's my next section.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at page 7 of your statement, paragraph 36, you indicate that you regularly coordinated activity with the SUP and OUPs organs in your area. By this do you mean jointly patrolling the cities and the roadways and check-points and the like, or are you talking about something else? If it's something else, please give me details of what this activity with the specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a long enough question. Your questions are much, much longer than anybody else's, and they contain so much verbage it's unnecessary. Just have a look at the page that's on the transcript at the moment. Let's try and be sharp with these questions for the witness. It doesn't help the witnesses either to understand when you go on for so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've trying to get a lot of information in a very short period of time with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you must --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- Short circuit these proceedings. So we have a lot of information, there's a lot of information contained in the statement that I need to set up for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't need to keep repeating yourself which you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's deal with that particular question, Mr. Mitic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was always coordination and it could be implemented at one of the command posts or at an observation post or elsewhere, whatever the two commanders involved happened to meet, or anyone responsible for exercising command. It was most little the case with the commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade, to some extent with the sector organs from the defence ministry and to some extent with members of the MUP if there was anything that was really important for any future activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. I'm specifically talking about the SUPs and the OUPs, sir. And I apologise, it's difficulty in the translation; but the secretariats of the interior and the "odvajanje," or detachments of the interior that you mention specifically in paragraph 36. Surely you're not saying the OUPs were engaged in the activity with the 549th Motorised Brigade the regular police offices, the police stations.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 36 states this in no uncertain terms coordination was carried out with the 549th Motorised Brigade with the command of the 55th Border Battalion with the chief of the Prizren district. If it was necessary to do this in relation to the authorities or anything. Municipality presidents, organs of the Ministry of Interior, the Prizren SUP, Suva Reka, Gora and Orahovac, as well as those of our units that were lower-ranking units the MUP too had its secretariats and within these secretariats it had detachments. And the same thing applied to the district organs, that they also had their own detachments in the districts, territorial districts, and they had departments or recruitment offices in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now specifically with respect to your coordinated activity with the SUP and OUPs organs, did this mean that you were jointly patrolling the cities, jointly patrolling the roadways, and jointly maintaining check-points?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units belonging to military territorial detachments were never in settled areas, populated areas. They were normally in one of the broader areas guarding vital facilities or mountain passes. Sometimes that important traffic intersection and wherever they had been assigned in order to guard and secure some facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only left the populated areas on about by the 25th of April 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You overlapped there, Mr. Ivetic. You'll need to start that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that the military territorial detachment units, specifically the ones from the Prizren zone, vacated or withdrew from settled areas only by the 25th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the mobilisation, each of the military territorial districts took up its positions according to a previously existing plan. It remained at those positions until it was ordered to do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now could you answer my question. Do you recall if that meant that the last of these units left settled areas only by the 25th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 108th detachment, if it was attached to the 549th Brigade, it went with that brigade to a different sector. It certainly didn't stay in the town or in any of the populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, did this occur around the 25th of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was throughout the war, up until the very end when certain units returned to the fold of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that in fact the military territorial detachment units, in fact the units from your zone in Prizren, did have authorisation and indeed specific orders for protecting the civilian population, particularly if they found themselves within your zone of combat?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military department is not in charge of defending the civilian population. There were other people who were in charge of that. Its only responsibility was to secure and guard its territory, and this was the main task for each of the military territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I draw your attention to 5D1004, a one-page document dated the 20th of April, in Pristina, by the command of the military district in Pristina, and Colonel Pesic. If you look at item number 2 of this order, it talks about military territorial detachment units being tasked with finding safest locations for evacuating civilians, protect them from combat. Do you recall now that, in fact, the military territorial department in Pristina did authorise military territorial detachment units to safeguard and protect civilians?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order is clear given the fact that some refugee columns and families were returning to certain populated areas. It says here that the commanders should get in touch with the authorities in order to find room where they would put up these people each in their own area, of course. And once these people were put up, if a village, for example, was abandoned and people returned to that village, of course this was something that needed to be secured. As for guarding the population, safeguarding the population, this again was someone else's task, but the military territorial unit would stay in the broader area of that particular village if this was in fact its combat assignment, or perhaps a different unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding the members of the military territorial detachment units, can you tell us if the conscripts composing these units came from the territory of the whole municipality, that is to say, were they from the urban areas?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for keeping up the manpower levels in military territorial detachments depending on their military speciality, if you had, for example, a recruit who had a better level of training, he could have been from any of the areas within the Prizren district, but as a matter of principle, he would work for Gora, because all people from Gora were in the Gora military territorial detachment which covered the whole Gora area. The same applied to Suva Reka and Prizren. And it wasn't just from the town. It was from all the villages in this municipality and possibly also the neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when these units were not engaged, when they had leave or time off, did they sleep in a joint location or some sort of barracks, or did they return to their own private homes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All military conscripts that had their accommodation organised based on their locations. There were no more barracks after the mobilisation but room would be provided for their accommodation in each of the areas covered by a certain military territorial detachment depending on where the units were involved. These were individual units, small units, that could be put up outside under tents or perhaps in buildings that had been abandoned or in a company facility or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we heard earlier from Colonel Pesic that there were four different types of VJ green uniforms. What particular uniform did your military territorial detachment units have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the military department wore the M-83 camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall if any of the units from your zone were comprised, that is the military territorial detachment units, were comprised of any conscripts from villages such as Mala Krusa in the Orahovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part the components there of the 101st Military Detachment in Velika Krusa, in Mala Krusa, in Orahovac, in Opterusa, in Zutiste [phoen], Retimlje [phoen] outside those places in the broader area, practically from Zrze to Malisevo and then down the depth all the way to Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Suva Reka. Do you recall if in Suva Reka you had an officer within the military territorial detachment by the name of Dr. Boban Vuksanovic and if so can you recall what his duties or position were?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boban Vuksanovic earlier served as president of Suva Reka municipality. He was a physician. He was mostly in the military territorial detachment where he was a doctor in the command, and he held a certain rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe we still have 5D1004 on the screen, and I think -- we've already covered that. I'll move on to another one. If we look at -- if we look at 5D372 for a moment. This is an order dated the 22nd of April, 1999. And if we look at part 1 of the document once it comes up on the screen. It's a one-page document. Sir, does this refresh your recollection, in fact, that military territorial detachments, prior to the end of April, 1999, were in fact in part located within inhabited settlements?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such units in residential areas. All of my units were outside of residential areas or settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we look now to another topic. In your statement at paragraph 23, which for those who are following is page 5 of the English and the Serbian, sir, you state that MUP organs engaged conscripts who were on wartime assignment to uphold order. Are you actually saying the MUP engaged its reserve component which is made up of persons who are conscripts assigned to the MUP in compliance with the laws?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1998, there were military conscripts from war units within the units belonging to the Ministry of the Interior. Those were mostly people who joined the organisation voluntarily, without the consent of military departments. We have a specific -- some specific cases that -- where some conscripts were killed within the units of MUP, whereas their wartime assignment was in the units of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that -- sir, wouldn't you agree with me that your office would have to handle all military conscripts for both the Ministry of Interior and the Pristina Corps? How is it possible that you permitted conscripts to, as you say - now, I don't want to misquote you - without the content of your department?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for joining MUP units was that members of the MUP units had selected these people without a prior consent of the military department. Later on there came an order that such military conscripts should return to their units. I don't know what the reasons for that were, but at the time they were under the MUP command. They wore their clothes and their weapons, and upon returning them, they returned to their wartime units. The military department was unable to exercise control over that because they did not know who joined which unit. It wasn't until later that they found this out about specific cases, or it wasn't until these people returned the weapons that they were issued with that they went back to their original units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said that this was -- I believe in your statement you identify when mobilisation occurred, so I will not going into that. If -- strike that. At paragraph 33 of your statement, you state that although cooperation with the Ministry of Interior was good throughout the war, their units were not resubordinated to you. First of all, Colonel, I would like to know if in fact you believe that there were specific units of the MUP that were supposed to be resubordinated to your department in Prizren under the applicable laws.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for somebody to be resubordinated to me. It's more logical to have me resubordinated to somebody else, and for something like that I needed the consent of the commander of the military department in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say it was more logical to have you resubordinated to somebody else, you're not implying that you expected to be resubordinated to the Ministry of Interior, are you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I would be resubordinated to them when I belonged to the army and they are part of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, sir. I was just clearing something up that came out differently in English. Now, if -- one moment, please. I might have just one or two more questions for you if I can just -- for a moment. Colonel, thank you for your time. I think we've covered all the topics that I had planned to cover with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Mitic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mitic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could get P1415 up on e-court, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mitic, you said in your statement that you received a copy of that order. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The order -- and I just want to get the chain of command right. From your standpoint the order -- the original order was made by the 3rd Army command, and then the Pristina Corps command on the basis of that order sent an order to the military territorial departments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the Pristina Corps. It is most likely that this document was received by the command of the military district in Pristina, and then the command of the military district further issued orders to their military departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the last page of the document, you'll see that it was supposed to be delivered to the Prizren military department. That is your military department.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is most likely a case where the order of the Pristina Corps was signed by Major-General Vladimir -- no, no. I apologise. By Major Pavkovic, yes. The order should have been written most likely -- not most likely, but according to the law by the commander of the military district. I see that this was added in pen. It wasn't typed. And most likely they had some technical difficulties whereby the same order was forwarded to military departments. I remember well that as they started implementing this order I received it verbally from my commander, and he said that a written order would follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English translation has you referring to a person as Major Pavkovic. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major-General signed. Commander Major-General Pavkovic, and the first name Nebojsa is not visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The order is for the mobilisation and training of military conscripts in village units, and if you look at paragraph 3 on the first page, you will see that it states that you should devote special attention to security measures, secrecy and camouflage discipline in carrying out this task. In arming military conscripts ostensibly for the defence of Serbian villages, do you know why it should be done in secret?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was aimed at carrying out organisational and technical preparations for distribution of weapons, which means that the entire weaponry had to be prepared in advance. It had to be prepped. It had to be distributed to units, and lists had to be prepared for all conscripts that were to be issued with weapons. Further on, they had to ensure that all of it was done in accordance with the legal provisions, that all the lists were drawn up according to the rules about how weapons are to be issued to conscripts. They had to take into account how many conscripts there were in the territory because a large number of them were absent, and they were to be informed in time that weapons were to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And did doesn't say here -- the order doesn't specify when this issuing of weapons was to be conducted. This was something that the commanders had to decide once they received orders from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You haven't really focused on what I'm asking. You have discussed various items of the document. I'm going to come back to the question I asked you, but just look at the second page of the document, paragraph 10. It reads here: "The deadline for distribution of weapons is until 1800 hours on the 1st of July, 1998, and readiness for defence of settlements is by 1800 hours on the 3rd of July, 1998." So there was a deadline, but the question I'm asking you again is do you know of any reason for the secrecy in carrying out what you say and this order ostensibly say is a legal action? And I wanted to focus on the reason for the secrecy. That's all I'm asking you about now.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All preparations have to be secret. That's the basic rule. In order for weapons to be distributed, the deadline for preparations was the 1st of July, 1998, up until 1800 hours, and that's what I told you needed to be done. And if the mobilisation is not carried out, then nothing else can be done. Once the mobilisation is carried out, then a plan is made for combat operations, and this must be secret because all preparations have to be secret. We were expecting that there would be an escalation in developments in Kosovo and Metohija involving Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many weapons were distributed in your area, in the Prizren area of responsibility pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that period of time, I did not distribute weapons except to the individuals who were key persons for implementing certain tasks such as, for example, the temporary group, the couriers who were armed. There were perhaps 10 to 20 such people, such conscripts, in each municipality, and later on they typically joined military territorial detachment. The rest of the weapons were stored in the depot of 549th Brigade, and it was distributed once the mobilisation was announced and carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to return to P14, to this document, but if we could have a look at P931, and then we will get back to it. We have evidence before the Court that 47.000, or thereabouts, sets of these weapons were distributed at about that time. If you look at page 23 of this document. Is it there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I think that the witness cannot give us relevant information concerning the minutes from these sessions of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, because that's several levels above him. He can only speculate about these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask him to speculate. I'm going to ask him one or two specific questions, if he knew something. And I'm going to -- well, first I'll ask him to link what is in the minutes to the document 1415, and then I'll ask him what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear the question. If you really think you need to refer to this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't. Perhaps I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know why people don't here say, Look, one the collegium minutes recorded 47.000 weapons being issued can you help us on that matter or more specifically. Why we have to dig up the documents knowing how long it takes to put them on the screen in this situation I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My purpose was, you know, in seeing the document. In this case the witness might be a little bit more cooperative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's for you to decide on that, make that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I haven't found it so far personally a successful method of dealing with the situations in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At a collegium meeting, and that is a meeting of the senior staff of the VJ, in February 1999, General Samardzic, who was the 3rd Army commander in July and June of 1998, said that 47.000 weapons had been issued for the defence of the Serbian villages pursuant to his order and that the role of these armed persons was to defend the villages and participate with army units in any operations in the immediate vicinity. Firstly, having regard to what General Samardzic said he ordered and how many weapons he said were distributed, can you say how many weapons were distributed in the Prizren zone of responsibility pursuant to this order in 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you literally that only temporary units and key persons who were very important in the course of mobilisation were issued with weapons. As for arming the population, that was done by the Ministry of Defence through their field departments and sections. I can't give you any figure concerning the Prizren district which has four municipalities. I can't tell you who issued weapons and how many weapons there were out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't it your function under this order, and this order of the 26th of June, to prepare and organise these units for the defence of these settlements? What is it a function of the military department to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the answer, could we get back to P1415.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could conduct training only with my own units while the preparations were carried out until the mobilisation. What we could do was take out a unit to shooting grounds to train them on the capabilities of weapons, to carry out various preparations. If we had ammunition, we could actually practice shooting, and then later on weapons had to be cleaned and stored in depots. That's the kind of training that I conducted with my units. And the same applied to war units, except that there was no requirement to carry out preparations concerning field or branch departments. As for the Ministry of the Interior, sometimes they joined trainings if they had some senior officers who needed training, and if we were able to provide assistance to them, then we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 6 of this order, it says: "After completing the distribution," and that is the distribution of the weapons, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, light machine-guns, sniper rifles, et cetera, noted in paragraph 2 so paragraph 6 to continue: "After completing the distribution, prepare and organise inhabited places for defence. The military departments commanders are responsible for organising this in their zones of responsibility in cooperation of the MUP and local self-government organs." And it says: "Form units in each village according to the military structure ... appoint a commander, deputy and assistant for each unit." And if you look at page 2 in the English, also page 2 in the B/C/S, at paragraph 9 it states: "Responsibility for these tasks: Unit commanders for the distribution of weapons and military department commanders for forming and training of units in these settlements." Now, from what you're saying, I take it that you -- let me ask this question. What was this role, having regard to this order, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat that this is an order for preparations. I was unable to call up the entire military department. I neither had the money nor time or the abilities to do that. All of this pertains to organisation and preparations for what might occur later in the year. So preparations were to be carried out without calling up reserve forces. We had to designate commander and then other senior officers, staff, and so on. All of this is called preparations, and that had to be carried out on paper without actually calling up conscripts to attend a certain gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I've already showed you paragraph 10, the last paragraph where a deadline is set out, deadline for you to complete your part. Are you saying that as command of the Prizren district or Prizren military district you did nothing pursuant to this order, notwithstanding the deadline?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I carried out all the preparations by the 1st of July, 1998, at 1800 hours. I reported to my commander that I had carried out the preparations. This does not mean that I actually distributed the weapons. I completed all the preparations by that deadline, and there were two days left for combat readiness. And I would have to receive an order as to what unit to call up, and I would have to issue that unit with their task on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please read aloud paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The deadline for the distribution of weapons is up to the 1st of July, 1998 at 1800 hours, and readiness for defence of settlements is by 1800 hours on the 3rd of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, listen carefully to this question: Can I take it from what you've said that the first part of that paragraph does not mean what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe there was a unit that was mobilised from the composition of the Pristina Corps or the military district, but my units had not been mobilised by that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first part of it, about the deadline for the distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in the previous item -- or, rather, in a previous item, two or three, it says that commanders will decide on the readiness of units. This refers in general to units that had already been mobilised as some probably had because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please address the issue, don't dance around the subject. The words simply say in 10 that there's a deadline for distributing weapons, and that deadline is 1800 hours on the 1st of July. It's not a deadline for preparing or drawing up preparations for the distribution of weapons. It's a deadline for distributing weapons. Now, have we to understand that that does not mean what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it does, because then it would say distribute weapons on the 1st of July up to 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what it says. That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, it doesn't. It says deadline for the distribution of weapons. So that's the deadline before the distribution, and the distribution will take place when an order was issued as to what unit and at what time. When my commander tells me orally or by telegram, "Call up unit 108th Territorial Detachment and distribute weapons to them," that's an order in my book, and I await such orders throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be a strange difference between English and Serbian in this respect then. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, I'm afraid I don't understand what you've been saying. Firstly, the order, and I won't take you through the order, where the order does not give unit commanders as you indicated earlier any discretion in this, it states quite clearly in paragraph 2 to distribute the weapons. It states in paragraph 3 to make lists before distributing the weapons. And it states on the basis of the list call up military conscripts in small groups to the army barracks or organise distribution and issue of weapons in Serbian and Montenegrin villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, if you got a letter saying the deadline for paying your rent is the 1st of July, would that mean you don't have to pay it until after the 1st of July in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the 20th and the 29th also, but the final deadline is the 1st, and after that, if you don't pay, your electricity's cut off. But this is something else. I have to listen to orders coming from my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- before I move on, this is the last question, do you know at all, whether any weapons at all were distributed in your zone at any time as a result of this order?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that we distributed some of the weapons, but all the weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To all the weapons, that is 2.200 barrels, were distributed after a state of emergency was declared and after mobilisation was declared, which was in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. You're saying as a result of this order -- or pursuant to this order, June 1998, you distributed the weapons in March 1999? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the weapons for the entire military district, that is 2.200 barrels, were distributed only after the mobilisation on the 24th and 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some weapons, the most necessary ones, were given to the temporary units and units which had to immediately be attached to a brigade, but not to everyone in the units, only the key people whose duty it was to carry out mobilisation in order to secure the call-up posts, and the weapons would be distributed either in the barracks or in the mobilisation points but mostly in the barracks, in the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, did you have any weapons to -- to give a weapon to everyone who would answer the call-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had complete artillery weapons [as interpreted] except for mortars and recoilless guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But every -- every soldier who answered the call-up was given a light weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what happened to the weapons for the 26.000 Albanians who didn't respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They weren't in the reserves of any unit of the army except for those who had a wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you tell us they would not be given weapons until they were mobilised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Some were armed, but most were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if the 26.000 Albanians had turned up in response to your call-up, you would have given each one a weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not -- I could only give weapons to those who were on my wartime assignment, and the command of 549th to their people, and the MUP to their people. Everybody to their own men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your statement says that 26.000 Albanians did not respond to the call-up in the district of Prizren. By that you mean the department of Prizren, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The whole department, for all four municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you -- you would not be responsible for issuing the weapons to these 26.000 if they had arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not responsible for that, nor did I have the barrels. My formation was specific, and for each unit and each person it was well known what weapons they were to be issued with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So paragraph 2 of this order which is on the screen was not instructing you to issue light weapons to all conscripts in your department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was only for military conscripts in my units. Beyond that, I was not authorised to arm anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by your units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My units numbered 2.200 men according to the wartime establishment, and those were the units at my disposal, and there were some who were not included in any establishment units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see to whom this order is addressed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I take it from -- from your evidence so far that you are basically saying that the order on the 26th of June wasn't implemented at all before mobilisation in March 1999. Wasn't the military territorial units responsible for resupplying these local defence units with ammunition during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question doesn't sufficiently identify who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't your military territorial department --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was your military territorial department responsible for replying these local defence units with ammunition during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. I don't think the expression is "military territorial department," Mr. Stamp. I think it's military department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the "territorial" applies to the active detachments, the units who actually carry out activities. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just a correction that I feel should be made in the transcript. In the transcript on page 26, in line 2, the witness said -- he didn't say artillery weapons, he said "strejecko ranuzanje" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is? Unfortunately, the interpreter has given us the word in B/C/S. So what do you say the translation should be? Sorry, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Maybe "infantry weapon," not "artillery weapon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Or "light weapon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go to P1139 in e-court. And while it's coming up, Mr. Mitic, the question is: Wasn't the Pristina military department involved in resupplying these village defence units with ammunition during the course of 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina military district was not competent for that. It was the administration of the Ministry of Defence from Pristina through their departments. They had six departments on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and in each one they had these departments depending on the number of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document there on e-court before you, P11139, is the -- is a report of the Pristina military department command of the 26th of September, 1998, and I represent to you, sir, that it is signed by the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Djordjevic, Miodrag Djordjevic. I don't think you can see that on your page, but that is the next page of the document indicates that. If you look at paragraph 9 -- sorry, paragraph 8.4, you will see in the second to last paragraph it speaks about the activities of the defence forces, the Serbian defence forces in the village. And if you look further down at paragraph 12, you will see that the commander requests, and I'll read it: "Please issue a decision specifying the manner in which to resupply ammunition that our conscripts engaged in the defence of Serbian villages and population [sic] areas spent while fighting against the Siptar terrorists." Sir, I'll ask the question again and invite your answer having regarding this document signed by the command of the Pristina military department. Wasn't the Pristina military department involved in the resupply of ammunition to these village defence units during 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This in specific terms is the Pristina military department, not the Prizren military department, but what they did I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- did your military -- or did your unit, the Prizren military department, engage in resupply of ammunition to these village defence units in 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to something else. You said, at paragraph 59 of your statement, the last paragraph, that your -- that no mosques were destroyed in your zone, or there were over 30 mosques in Prizren and not a single one was demolished. Now, incidentally, when you say "in Prizren," do you mean your area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of the Prizren military department?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are over 30 mosques of various sorts in Prizren, and in all the villages inhabited by Albanians or Muslims there are mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you speak of "in Prizren," you're speaking about in the town of Prizren, or are you speaking about --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Prizren. The town itself has about 30 mosques. When I had some free time, I stood on top of the hill and counted them, and every village has a mosque except for the Catholic area where there are Catholic churches and the Serb areas where there are Serbian Orthodox churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I have a look at P01803, and when it comes up, Mr. Mitic, do you know the Prizren municipality mosque - that's the major mosque in Prizren - at Landovica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably was until the military operations. It is in the area of the military department, but I saw that mosque when I went to visit the monument of Boro and Ramiz. I know it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I ask if you know that mosque. Before you is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never inside a mosque, so I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mosque. In Prizren. This is a major mosque in Prizren? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the mosque in Prizren. The main mosque in Prizren I know. I know which one it is. It was -- there was a church there, Bogorodica Jevicka [phoen], Our Lady, which was then converted into a mosque, and I know where the main church and the main mosque are in Prizren. They're in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recognise this --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All mosques look alike. This one is unfinished, I think. I don't know which one this is. This is not the mosque from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the previous sentence the witness began answering the question but he was interrupted by Mr. Stamp. It has, however, been clarified with the second question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My question is you're not familiar, I take it, with the mosque at Landovica in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Landovica is, I think, about 10 or 15 kilometres away from Prizren. That's not in Prizren. It's on the territory of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're not familiar with that mosque?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the mosques in the other towns in the -- in your area of responsibility? For example, Celine in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the mosque --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I thought the witness had said that his paragraph 59 was confined to the town of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why are you asking questions about something he's not given any -- do you need more positive evidence from him about -- about these? I can't stop you if that's why you're doing it, but if you're challenging something, you're tilting at windmills.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke -- or you were asked some questions earlier about the reserve police squads. And while we're at it, could we bring up 5D985. Your department was involved in the mobilisation of members of the reserve police squads in 1999, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document in front of you is an order of the Pristina military district command.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we have a look at the last -- well, it's -- firstly it's dated 17th of April, 1999. And if we have a look at the last page, in paragraph 8 you said one of the tasks that you were to focus on or your -- it was being reported up that you were to focus on was the call-up of conscripts who are in the MUP reserve forces for the reserve police squads. Are you saying again that this was something that the Pristina military district command was involved in but for some reason your area, Prizren, wasn't involved in it, or were you involved in the call-up of conscripts for the MUP reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior have their own courier system which they use to call up their own conscripts. This is not something that the military department did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make a -- if I can make a suggestion to have the witness perhaps reads the particular line that Mr. Stamp is referring to, because I believe the English translation is incorrect on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, I should probably have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 8 there? Before -- could you read the third item of paragraph 8. Can you read it aloud, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about line three? It reads: "Calling up military conscripts who are in the reserve forces of the MUP," which means they went there without the military department knowing about this, and now they're supposed to be called up to join a war unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just read, do not interpret, and read what you see written there again for me please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Calling up military conscripts who are in the reserve forces of the MUP as RPO," which means they already are serving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the proper English translation would be the members of the military conscripts who are already in the reserve forces. That is what it means in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a great pity that the witness can't just read the words that are there, and we will have them translated. Would you now please just read the words that are in that line. Don't try to interpret it. Just read it in Serbian, please, and read it aloud. Please read, Mr. Mitic. Read it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. "Calling up military conscripts who are in the reserve forces of the MUP (as RPO)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last bit has not been translated and quite rightly so because you weren't asked to give us any comment. Mr. Stamp, we need to break, do we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, we need to have a break at this stage. Please leave the courtroom with the usher while we do that. And we will resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, do you know how many reserve police squads detachment there were in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many such detachments there were. I do know that each village was supposed to have one comprising two or three men. Specifically in my area of responsibility, when I toured my units, I observed between five and seven such detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your area of responsibility included Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Prizren, and Goran municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you observed five to seven detachments in that area?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area there were few villages that were ethnically pure. Therefore, maybe there was no need for more detachments such as those to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 49 of your statement, and while we're at it, could we bring up 5D991. Please look at the last paragraph of that document. You'll see that a criminal report was filed by the military police organs of the Kosovo Mitrovica military department. Was it the responsibility, and I'm asking you generally, was it the responsibility of the military departments to file criminal reports against civilians where they found civilians committing criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the responsibility of the military department to bring people in if they found someone committing a criminal offence. If they did, this person to be temporarily detained and then reported to the MUP, and then the MUP would take any further steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mitic, help me to be clear about certain things. The expressions "military district" and "military department" have been used by you. In Kosovo, how many military districts were there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo there was one military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Carry on if it's more complicated.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Pristina military district. It was the military district command in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in wartime?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in wartime it would take up its own wartime establishment, and it had quite many units. And military departments were in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. That's all I want in answer to that question. My next question is: How many military departments were there in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Name them, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina, Kosovska Mitrovica, Pec, Gnjilane, and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. When it came to mobilisation, was that the responsibility of the military district or the responsibility of the military departments?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military district would have been the most responsible body. They mobilised their own units, and military departments mobilised their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, help me to understand the difference between a unit in the military district and a unit in the military department.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military district, in addition to the command, also had units that were carrying out work on the ground, larger units. I won't know what the establishment was for these units, but in addition to all these units they also had a military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement, in English it says: "One of the main task of military --" there it says "military territorial departments was to mobilise war units and bring them up to strength." Now, my understanding so far is that one of these bodies, military district or military department, is responsible for mobilising men to provide men for both the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that the -- is that the district or the department?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, departments and the military district command. This task was performed through the keeping of military records, and these existed in all military departments from entering a file into the military record to actually deploying men to certain military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need the details, Mr. Mitic. I just want to get the system clear in my mind. Take, for example, the 549th Motorised Brigade. Do you know which department or district was responsible for mobilising troops that would be sent to serve with the 549th once war was declared?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the number of able-bodied conscripts up to the age of 35, I would select certain files from my record, and I would bring up to strength some elements of the 549th Brigade. Given the fact that throughout the territory they weren't sufficient military conscripts to bring that unit up to strength, the 549th Motorised Brigade was brought up to strength by applying the territorial principle from other district --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Was it your responsibility as the Prizren department to deal with providing further strength to the 549th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to the extent that I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example of an organ -- rather, a unit of the VJ that the Pristina military district was responsible for supplying troops to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing the same problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bringing all war units up to strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer my question. Identify for me, please, a unit of the VJ that it was their responsibility to try to strengthen.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was any such thing, because strength came from other military district outside Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bear in mind I'm trying to understand the difference between the job done by the district and the job done by the department. I think I'm beginning to understand better what the department does. I'm at a total loss to understand what the district did directly in relation to the mobilisation of men.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military department had the responsibility to bring up to strength war units in its own territory with as much manpower as was available; and then at the level of the military districts, there would be coordination. And if there were military conscripts in another municipality, then one could use that manpower from that municipality to bring the 549th Brigade up to strength. If there was none available then one had to go to military districts outside Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have told us about the military territorial detachments within your department. Were there any military territorial detachments which were the direct responsibility of the Pristina military district?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think during the war they had such detachments and units, that they set them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why were there military territorial detachments at all?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military territorial detachments are a component of the military department. The military department has its own command and independent units, and depending on why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's my question: Why. Is the army not sufficient for the purpose, the regular army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it has its own role within the army. Military territorial detachments are a component of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, some re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, it's me again. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P1415.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please look at item 2 at page 1 of this document. You were shown this document by my learned friend from the OTP. In your evidence you mentioned that you could not distribute weapons or ammunition without an order by the commander. What about item 2? Does it not seem to confirm what you said? If necessary, go through it. It's the latter part of item 2 that really matters.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "According to the orders of unit commanders, distribute" and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's not go any further than this.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand what it says, according to the orders of the commander, of course I can't do that immediately, but I can once the conditions are in place and once I had received from order from my commander because this is an order by the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any such orders prior to March 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aside from this one I received no other orders, except I was told. And then when the team from the military district toured us, I was informed about this, but then again it says according to an order by the commander, and my commander is the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us dwell on this a bit longer. In paragraph 8, if I'm not mistaken, of your statement, you talked about territorial defence, about the weapons and equipment left behind. Do you know that in 1994 the Law on Defence was passed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps remember whose responsibility it was after the Territorial Defence, after the Territorial Defence was abolished, to distribute weapons? Do you perhaps remember that, sir? Which state body was now in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that military departments and districts were set up in 1991, and the Territorial Defence was abolished in 1992. From that point on, there was no more Territorial Defence. Rather, there were now military departments and local bodies of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the Ministry of Defence had any responsibility in terms of distributing weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if again you can help me to understand this. Could you look, please, at P1115. I don't know how you would characterise this document. It's a sort of memo, and it comes, apparently, from General Lukic to SUP -- SUPs in -- or throughout Kosovo, and it refers to "... extracts from the register of weapons issued by the army to citizens engaged in reserve police stations to defend villages and cities in the municipalities ..." Now, you're aware of a register of weapons issued by the army to citizens engaged in reserve police stations, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the records of military conscripts in reserve forces, that's something that's kept by the Ministry of the Interior in relation to all of their units, including reserve police units. It seems that the lists were not updated here, so they were asking for a new register of citizens who had been issued weapons by the army. If they joined the ministry of the interior, they had to return the weapons to the army if they had received it originally from the army. And as for the army, we had records as well in military departments. We had our records, and our military conscripts were sometimes joined MUP, either on -- through a regular procedure or through an extraordinary one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read the first sentence of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Please find enclosed extracts from the register of weapons issued by the army of Yugoslavia to citizens in municipalities in the territory of your secretariat. This pertains to citizens engaged in reserve police stations to defend villages and cities. So far, the register was incomplete. The register has been compiled --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's enough. Earlier we had the reference RPO, and I think it was translated then reserve police units. Now, can I have the assistant of the interpreters, please. What is the correct translation of the expression that's in the first sentence of this referring to reserve police something or rather?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, PO stands for "policijsko odeljenje". It could be a police squad or a police station, depending on the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you accept, do you, Mr. Mitic, that you would be responsible for issuing -- sorry, that the army would be responsible for issuing weapons to citizens engaged in reserve police squads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in relation to all. We sent to the secretariats the lists of our conscripts who had wartime assignments with us. What this involved now was that if these conscripts, if they had been issued weapons by the army, they had to return those weapons to the army. Those who received weapons from the MUP remained in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no suggestion in this document that these weapons have to be returned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All they're asking for here is for the lists, for the register to be updated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's the list of the weapons issued by the army, not those issued by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. But issued to the military conscripts who were members of the army and were also now in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what it says, I'm afraid, Mr. Mitic, but we have your comments. Mr. Cepic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to clarify something. Did your military department have problems with the conscripts who were members of the reserve police forces and who failed to return to the -- to your units, to military units?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These military conscripts, while they were in the military department units, were they issued with the weapons by the military departments?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, yes, and some, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were they duty-bound to return those weapons?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have problems in enforcing this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1998 we did not, and then in the beginning of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document, bear in mind, is July, I think, 1998, when there would be no problem. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time the military department did not need that military conscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, my colleague Mr. Ivetic asked you several questions and some things remained unclear, so I would like you to clarify them for me. He asked you whether conscripts from Mala Krusa, Krusa, Orahovac, Celine, whether you had people from those villages join your units. You answered in the affirmative and you said they were members of 101st Territorial Detachment in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me where the 101st Territorial Detachment was deployed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was deployed in the village of Zrze and in Bela Crkva in Orahovac, in an area near Malisevo, Vran Stena, Velika Hoca, Opterusa, and Retimlje along the depth of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was it deployed in settlements or outside of settlements?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only outside of settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These settlements that you mentioned, do they represent the borders of the area of responsibility of the 101st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any reserve police squads in that area?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ivetic asked you about the physician whose name was Boban.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vuksanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vuksanovic. Would you please tell me, do you know what happened to that physician during the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vuksanovic, son of Nadezda Bobek was a doctor before he was mobilised and then he served as a doctor during combat operations during the war. When there was no need for him to be present at the command headquarters I would release him so that he could go and work in Suva Reka at the medical centre there. What happened once was that the residents in the village of Musotiste were without medical assistance and without any food.
