In that broader region there was a company of the 70th Territorial Detachment of Suva Reka. They also ran out of food and water, and they needed medical assistance. The commander of the 70th Military Territorial Detachment, pursuant to my order, contacted authorities and established a convoy in order to provide assistance and provide food, water, and medical assistance. The doctor from the medical centre was asked to join this column, this convoy. This convoy set out in the morning hours towards Musotiste, and they were ambushed by terrorist forces in the sector of Sopina and Dubrava. In that convoy there was also Novica Djordjevic who was the commander of the detachment. Then there was a man called Antic from Lestane. He was a military conscript. And then there was another Antic and two more soldiers, so a total of four persons plus two military conscripts. Djordjevic, Vuksanovic, both Antics were killed in the ambush, and the soldiers were wounded. Ten minutes after that event, I set out by myself, went to the location, provided assistance, and the assistance that was intended for the village of Musotiste was not provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, it was on the 14th. I have the exact state in my statement. The 14th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me just follow up with a short question. Members of your units, did they provide assistance to civilians on other occasions as well?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, questions were put to you about personnel in your units. You said that you reinforced 509th Brigade as well as your units by 200-something members. I would like to know this: Were only Serbs mobilised or did only Serbs receive call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Gorani also received call-up papers and they established 68th Territorial Detachment in the territory of Gora. The Muslims from Sredacka Zupa were also called up and then they joined that detachment and 108th Detachment. They became members of those units. And of course Muslims from the other municipalities were called up as well. The Turks were also called up. There was one unit whose members were Turks and they defended the barracks of 549th Brigade. The Roma were also called up, especially those from Suva Reka, as were Montenegrins. And there were also Albanians, specifically in my command headquarters. I had three Albanians on top positions -- in top positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Who was your commander? Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Colonel Zlatomir Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And before that Vojkan Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in -- during the war when was the command of the military district Pristina resubordinated to the corps?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MITIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was in the latter part of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Mitic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Greetings to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Milos Mandic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he will be taken for the Prosecution by Mr. Sachdeva. I mention that because I also have a sad responsibility to mention that this will be the last appearance of Mr. Sachdeva in this trial as he, like others before him, moves on to greener pastures, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we wish him well there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please take the solemn declaration to take the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated] ... documents to General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good day.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To begin with, did you make a statement to the Defence team of General Lazarevic, which you signed on the 20th of January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have that statement before you now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did you ask me to make certain corrections in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ask me on the 21st of January, at a meeting attended by you and I, to enter corrections into paragraphs 28, 29, 30 as mentioned on the document dated the 21st of January, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, on the 22nd of January, did you ask me to enter corrections into the statement? And please look at the piece of paper you have before you. In paragraph 16, 20, 24, 28, 36, and 46.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, if I were to put to you today the same questions that were put to you when your responses were entered into the statement, would your answers be the same with the corrections you asked to be entered?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to request admission of the witness statement which exhibit number is 5D1391 with supplemental information sheet from 21st and 22nd January, which will be under the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far, has the witness looked at both of these supplemental sheets?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: They're in front of him right now in hard copy. And also during the conversation, actually interview which we had we together filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need to know what you get up in your own time, Mr. Cepic, but these two will have to be uploaded as supplements to 5D1391 if that's the way you choose to do it. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, exactly. Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour. May I continue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you look at paragraph 31 of your statement, please. You speak of independent actions in the areas of the villages of Celine and Nogavac and Hoca. Are you aware that the forces of the MUP and the VJ conducted their actions in that area in late March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell me the following: The area I've mentioned, was it a terrorist stronghold during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially in the second half of May. There was a situation where we had an armoured brigade in that area armed with the most up-to-date equipment that the VJ then had, and it was on a very shaky footing. Why? All the roads leading to Pristina from Orahovac were frequently mined at that time, and the vehicles with men on board ran into ambushes. We had enormous losses. I wish to point out that the terrorist forces were acting very professionally. In that period of time, there was a farm or a cooperative or whatever it was called --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: It was in that period in Orahovac, because of work being done in the vineyards that the farmers' cooperative, or whatever the enterprise was called, engaged eight tractor drivers to work in the vineyards. One day, they went missing. Before this action, on the 26th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to go into all this detail.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In the early morning hours from the direction of Celine, sniper fire was opened and two policemen were killed who were in a vehicle travelling on the Prizren-Djakovica road. In that period, the commander of the 3rd Army, the corps commander and the chief of the armoured mechanised unit branch of the VJ ran into an ambush and they themselves had an opportunity to see for themselves what the situation was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you look at paragraph 48 of your statement, please. The last page. I think you received an order from the Pristina Corps command for the accommodation and security of the civilian population and that the members of the VJ who were under your command treated the civilians humanely.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at 5D1072. General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: It's a daily combat report to the Pristina Corps command, dated the 20th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at item 11, paragraph 2, which begins with the words "The reception of refugees." Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: "In the Mixed Artillery Battalion sector, the reception of refugees began around 1900 hours. A mother with children and elderly Albanians from Jovic village." Should I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: They were transported in two vehicles and one bus in several trips. They were also provided with food, soldiers' rations and part of the packages of the conscripts from the mixed Artillery Battalion (food). Police guarded them at the school and then they were escorted to Dragobilje village from which they went to Jovic village."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, is this the only situation where you provided assistance to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No. While in that area, I continuously -- or, rather, we continuously, constantly, and within the limits of our ability provided assistance to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit 5D1071.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a daily combat report to the command of the Pristina Corps, dated the 24th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at item 4, "Security."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please read the first sentence under the heading.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: "Civilians in the brigade units' sectors are protected."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to know what this protection consisted in.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, this protection primarily consisted in ensuring necessities such as food, drinking water, health care, and personal security and security of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take a look at the fifth bullet point of the same item.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It begins with the words?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: "Strenuous efforts are made to take and carry out measures to protect the life and health of people as well as the implementation of measures pertaining to the International Law of War and the provisions of the Geneva Conventions on the treatment of prisoners of war and civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll put a general question to you now, General, concerning the war period. Was special significance attached to the protection of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, did the terrorist forces use civilians as human shields?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Defence Exhibit 5D973.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the English translation to come up, do you recognise the document, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a daily combat report to the command of the Pristina Corps. As I can't see the date, it's not legible, but it's approximately the 30th day from the beginning of the war. I conclude that by the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It says in the English translation 25th of April, 1999. Would that correspond to the date?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 1, 1.1 in the middle of that paragraph. It says: "From contacts -- we learned in contact with a person --"

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. "We learned in contact with a person from the refugee group that the Siptar terrorist forces are not allowing civilians to leave but are using them as a human shield."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was there more than one situation of this kind where civilians were misused by the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were always civilians who were in groups of refugees outside populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D974, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I do. This is a daily combat report to the command of the Pristina Corps. The date is the 27th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 4, "Security."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again you say: "Civilians in the brigade's sectors are protected."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the -- the order of the Pristina Corps command, were you creating the right conditions for putting up this civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 5D965.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just for the General to be able to see the B/C/S, could we please focus on the header, just for the date. Thank you. General, can you identify this document now, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was produced by the brigade command, and the date is the 4th of May, 1999, to the command of the Pristina Corps. This is a document which constitutes a response to a document by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your answer to item 2, specifically, I will not be reading it, you name a number of sectors where it would be possible to take in new temporarily displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why these villages for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Simply because there were no terrorist forces in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, when you arrived in the area what was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In that area the villages had by and large been abandoned, deserted, very few people remaining there. In a way you could tell who they were because of their enormous fear of war. My officers would talk to them, and what we were focusing on was to establish a climate of mutual trust, because these were local civilians who were nationals of Serbia. And of course, when we started speaking to them this bond of trust could not be established immediately but gradually, but contact was establish; and they realised that we were doing our best to help them get on with their lives and work. In terms of food, necessities, medical supplies were paramount, for example, and we knew, in the roughest of terms, that they were in touch with people who were in refugee groups in the area, and we asked them to speak to these people, and when they spoke to these people to try to get them to return to their homes and get on with their lives and go about their regular jobs and activities to the extent possible. We also said that we would help them as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did some people start returning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the second supplemental information, who actually translated that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My assistant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to do something about an official translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't read well in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do my best, and we will contact translation service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem with that is that the witness is here and should be confirming the accuracy of his statement while he's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Cepic, that the best way to do it this, regrettably, but we have time before we break again, is for you to ask the witness to read each of the changes that you've made. The reason I didn't do this earlier is I hadn't actually seen the second one until we came into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first supplemental information sheet from 21st of January, do I have to clarify something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not concerned about that. I think it's okay. It's the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can you have him read the changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And confirm that he's satisfied that they are accurately reflect what he wanted. It's very easy to ask him to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, would you please have a look at the supplemental information sheet dated the 21st of January. I would like to go through it. And please keep a copy of your statement open right next to it. We'll start with paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's actually -- the one I have is dated the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Actually, General and I had a meeting on 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first one is the 21st of January. This one starts with paragraph 16 and says: "The last sentence of the said paragraph should have the following ..." In my copy that's dated the 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Is the witness reading from one dated the 23rd or the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Actually, 22nd of January is dated at the top of the page, but it is probably filed on the -- in B/C/S version, but I will try with -- just to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can see it, there is the English version that we have, and it says 23rd on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My assistant made corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now let's read the various paragraphs, please. Ask the witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, will you please look at paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you not ask me to add the following words to that paragraph "According to sectors and defence positions"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20 -- please open that paragraph. Did you not ask me for the second sentence in that paragraph to read as follows: "Cooperation with the civilian authorities was carried out with the objective of taking care of the civilians and carrying out joint control of any movement in unpopulated areas and along the main roads"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you not ask me to enter the following amendment in relation to paragraph 24: "The units were toured and controlled of the 252nd Armoured Brigade by the superior command and chiefs of the mechanised and armoured units of the land forces sector of the General Staff of the VJ, Colonel-General Kovacevic"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The next one, paragraph 28, did you not say the following changes were required in relation to the last sentence after the comma: "However the forces of TG 252 stopped outside Dobra Voda village and the other component of TG 252 in the valley of the following villages: Bica, and Grabac, to the south-west of the villages of Brocna and Vocnjak at about five kilometres"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you not require that these sentences be added to that same paragraph: "MUP forces that we were lending support to did not go any further than those lines. The use of equipment in this action was exceptionally small and hardly any ammunition was expended. That was the very beginning of the NATO airstrikes, and for the most part the equipment was camouflaged and concealed"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you not ask me to enter an amendment to paragraph 36? Instead of the word "nine armoured vehicles," it should read "nine combat vehicles"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The last amendment that you requested, paragraph 46 of your statement, in addition to what was said another sentence which reads: "In order to sanitize the terrain, the VJ was authorised to do this in the border belt. Outside the border belt this was the responsibility and the obligation of the civilian authorities."

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. That does clarify one or two points that had been mistranslated. And it would be best if you did not upload the English version of the second supplementary information. You will have to upload the B/C/S version, obviously, but not the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Is it a proper time for the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mandic we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. While we have that break would you please leave the courtroom with the usher. We shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any further Defence examination? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to the corrections made in paragraph 28, I no longer have a cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Sachdeva. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I start can I just inquire, I understand that the documents that are mentioned in this statement that have not been shown to the witness are automatically admitted into evidence and some of them as far as our records can tell do not have translations. I take it they're not admitted up to the time translations are provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. -- General Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me start by asking you your -- your brigade, the 252nd Brigade, came into Kosovo and Metohija at the end of March; is that right? March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And upon that redeployment, you were responsible to the Pristina corps commander, General Lazarevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is it also right that the Tactical Group, the 252nd Tactical Group was also under your command and also under the command of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: It was not under my command, but it was under the command of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who commanded the Tactical Group of the 252nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Up to the 5th of April I did. After the 5th of April it was Colonel Miodrag Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So let me just be clear. After the 5th of April you had no responsibility whatsoever with respect to the Tactical Group of the 252nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were asked earlier on in examination-in-chief about the villages in Orahovac, and you were asked whether you knew whether there were terrorist strongholds in that area, and your response was, "Yes, especially in May." Can I just ask you when you say yes, do you mean from the onset of the war, in other words, from the 24th of March, 1999, or do you simply restrict your knowledge to -- from May up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: From the second half of May until the end of the war when operations began against the Defence forces of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were asked by counsel for the Defence as to whether you knew if the VJ and the MUP had conducted operations in Orahovac, and you answered no. I take it you're -- you maintain that evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you were redeployed to the area of Kosovo within the 252nd Brigade, and as you've said your commander was General Lazarevic, did you not have a briefing with General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In the period from April to June, I think I had two meetings or three meetings with General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let's just stick to the time of your movement, your deployment to -- to Kosovo and Metohija. When you moved there, did anyone from the Pristina Corps command brief you as to the state of operations in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Only in the zone of responsibility or the area of deployment in greater detail. In general, there was no time or opportunity to talk about the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it that you do know, at least now you do know, that at the end of March and the beginning of April there was a combat or several combat operations in the area of Orahovac municipality by the VJ and by the MUP. You know of that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I learned about that after the war from the materials available to me and also when preparing for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that even in the villages that you have spoken about, Celine, for example, and other villages in Orahovac there was -- well, those were the areas where you were deployed in May 1999. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In those villages which you mentioned, the brigade units were not deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I guess I'm finding it difficult to understand how you would not have received a briefing by the Pristina Corps command that in the area where you were to be deployed that there had -- you were not told that there had been VJ and MUP operations in that area. Can you enlighten us a bit further on that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In general operations were conducted, but as to the details of those combat operations, I did not have any special knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't think it would have been important for -- for you to have been told about those operations considering you were to be deployed in that area, in the same municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I received a task, and my task was to take up the areas I was ordered to take up in that part of the municipality and to organise defence. That was my main goal while I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You say in your statement the -- the date of deployment was the 29th of March. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain in greater detail what area you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the deployment from the 1st Army to the 3rd Army. In other words, to Kosovo and Metohija. I understand the decision was on the 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The decision was that on the 29th of March, up to 2400 hours, the brigade should be resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Wasn't there, however, a Mechanised Battalion from your brigade already present in Kosovo from the 16th of March, 1999, onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that this -- well, the Mechanised Battalion, what did it comprise of? Tanks, other heavy artillery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The Mechanised Battalion consisted of two weakened mechanised companies and a weakened tank company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how many tanks would there have been in that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is my understanding -- understanding right that they were deployed in the area of Srbica in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I can't reply to that question because I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, presumably the Mechanised Battalion of the 252nd Armoured Brigade was your responsibility. It came under your brigade, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: That was a unit from my brigade, but I was responsible for it until the date you mentioned in the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you've already told the Court that the battalion was indeed in Kosovo on the 16th of March, and so when that deployment took place, you must have been informed firstly as to the purpose, and secondly, as to the location. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: When units are resubordinated such information is not provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, and you are a general, are you seriously telling the Court that when a unit that you have command of is to be redeployed you as the brigade commander is not informed of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: We should draw a distinction here between relocation and resubordination. A unit is relocated and also resubordinated to another unit. From that point on it is under the care of whoever it is resubordinated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps I'm not making myself clear. I'm not after which units it was -- it became subordinated to. I'm talking about the timing when there was a decision to relocate these units, and you as the commander of those units must have been told, firstly, as to the purpose of the relocation, and secondly, the actual location where these units were to go. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your evidence is that seven tanks from your brigade that were relocated, taken away from your arsenal, and you had no idea about that. If that's your evidence, then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I knew they would be resubordinated to another unit. They were separated out, and then the unit to which they were resubordinated would take care of the men and their equipment from that point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, why were they -- well, now you're saying resubordinated, so I take it they were not relocated. Why were they being resubordinated to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decision of my superior command. It was from them that I received my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you received an order from your superior command as to the resubordination of these -- of this Mechanised Battalion. What did that order say to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall the details right now because of the lapse of time, but in that order, as in any order that deals with resubordination, it stated to whom, when, and where the unit would be resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you say you can't remember the details, you don't know to whom, and you don't know where. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I know to whom and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps you can tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The Mechanised Battalion was resubordinated to the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it's your understanding as -- as a brigade commander and as a general that at the time the -- let me suggest to you that the resubordination was part of a wider plan to destroy Kosovo Albanian terrorists in Kosovo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: What I knew while I was performing that duty was not so wide-ranging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I might interrupt just for a moment. The -- it's important that we establish whether the changes in the position taken by this witness are the result of translation problems or are, in fact, inherent in the evidence. So we shall require a formal translation of this evidence from page 66, line 11, to page 68, line 19. Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, when you received that order from your commander, your superior commander, and the resubordination took place, was there any discussion about a possible violation of the so-called October agreement whereby there was only a limited amount of military presence allowed in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: My place and role at that time was such that I was never included in such conversations, nor did I know what these conversations and documents, if any, from October were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're -- you're not aware of the so-called October agreement, the agreement between the VJ and the Kosovo Verification Mission, OSCE? You're not aware of this agreement or such agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to the best of my recollection there was another agreement signed in October. There were other signatories who signed the October agreement, and it's even named after the signatories. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real question here, Mr. Sachdeva, is that there was an agreement which had a particular provision that you may be concerned about. The exact name is not terribly important. I think Mr. Cepic may be suggesting we should call it by a particular name. Perhaps he'll give us the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that's the Prosecutor's job to identify the document at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've told us it's named by the -- named after the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can -- I can just ask a very simple question and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, from your earlier answers I take it that you were not aware of agreement that had the effect of restricting the military presence, the VJ military presence, in Kosovo at the time of the 16th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: What I knew while I was brigade commander was not so extensive. I didn't deal with that agreement, nor was it something I was concerned with in my work. So you cannot expect me to answer that question. If someone at a higher level signed the agreement, it was then up to him to make sure it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, Mr. Mandic, that you did not know that in October agreement had been reached that resulted in the retreat of VJ units into barracks and a restriction on the number of VJ personnel who could, at any given time, be out of barracks and active in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that my knowledge extends precisely to what you mentioned in your question to me. I did not know any details. My information came mostly from the media and from information sent along military lines, but I didn't know about the manner of implementation because it did not concern my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that I have misunderstood the evidence and -- and I will check carefully to ensure that that does not persist, but I thought it was common knowledge; and no doubt others will try to assist in clarifying my understanding. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, when your brigade was in Kosovo and you carried out military activities, am I right in understanding that Albanian men of military age were of particular certain to yourself and to the army, to your brigade, in terms that they -- they could be viewed as potential terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an order that you signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for P3074. Mr. President, there's no translation at this time. However, it's a short document, and I would like to ask the witness to read from the document. And of course a request for translation has been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, General, this is from the 23rd of April, 1999, and you'll see at the bottom that it is -- there should be another page. But you recognise this document as your document, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want you to look at the -- you'll see at the top half the page towards the middle there's a section which is -- which starts 1.2, and there's a sentence just above that, and it starts "Upa civila." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read that sentence out, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Let me just -- it says: "About one and a half kilometres from the village of Masera [phoen] in the direction of Klina there is a large group of civilians among whom are a large number of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, my question is why -- why did you see it as necessary to report that there were able-bodied men amongst this group of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Because in the groups and columns appearing at the time in that area there were many women, children, and elderly, but this time there were also able-bodied civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what you say about the groups and columns appearing where there were women and children and elderly, that's what happened, wasn't it? Typically the refugee columns would be comprised of women and children and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: And able-bodied civilians. It's really difficult to make that sort of assessment when you have a large group of people. It's very difficult to be precise about how many elderly, how many women, how many children. These columns, as a rule, comprised all different sorts of people and individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, if they did, then why didn't you mention in this report that there were women and children and elderly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Because probably this was the first time that younger civilians turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you have included this in your report to the Pristina command, the corps command, precisely because the presence of able-bodied men is potentially a danger to -- to your military. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No. As soon as they turned up in an open area with their fellow citizens and they were visible, I could conclude that they had probably run away in a bid to not be drafted into their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want to go back to what you said about the 252nd, the Tactical Group, and if I recall correctly, you were no longer in command of that group as of the -- as of early April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you were removed from the command, how -- how did that take place? Were you given an order? Were you told verbally?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And he told you this over the telephone or in person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: In person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was the reason he gave you as to why you were being removed from the command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The fundamental reason was the fact that my establishment post was that of the commander of the 252nd Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. We are not military persons in this court. Can you explain why then, still why would that mean that you would no longer command a tactical group that you had been commanding.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The Tactical Group was a temporary unit, and I was its temporary commander before it was established; but my basic duty was that of brigade commander. I had documents to show that I was appointed to that position, and I was receiving salary for that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So are you saying that when you were taken off the command of the Tactical Group, it ceased to exist? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: When I stopped being commander of the Tactical Group, this had nothing to do with its further existence or future existence. It had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So if members of the Tactical Group, whenever they conducted combat operations or if -- if members would have committed crimes, they would have been outside of your responsibility. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your examination I said that the Tactical Group was subordinated to the Pristina Corps command and not to the command of the 252nd Mechanised -- Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your brigade, the Armoured Brigade, was subordinated to the Pristina Corps command during the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that -- and I appreciate what you say about the 252nd Tactical Group being part of the Pristina Corps, the corps that you were part of, but you must have been aware of allocations that members of the Tactical Group had committed serious war crimes during the time that you were present in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: The Tactical Group and the 252nd Armoured Brigade had different tasks, and they were working along different axes. Therefore, as to what was going on in the Tactical Group, this wasn't something that I could know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. Can we have a foundation for the submission made by my learned friend that members of the Tactical Group, 2P2 -- 252, committed serious war crimes during their time in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And actually I -- my question was actually not quite like that. My question was of allegations that there was war crimes were committed. It's actually been transcribed wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's close enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In any event, I refer to Exhibit 3D1061. I refer to the evidence of Mr. Vasiljevic. I understand his statement is P2594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm satisfied you have adequate foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I'm finding it difficult to understand, and again I appreciate that as of the beginning of April the Tactical Group was no longer under your command, however, within the Pristina Corps command, that you were not aware of serious -- of allegations of serious crimes committed by, if I put it this way, your former subordinates. You must have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No, because I had no contact with officers belonging to the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you say on this issue, you talk in your statement in paragraphs 48 and 50 at the end about the -- the fact that your soldiers adhered to the norms of international humanitarian law and protected civilians. That's the evidence you've given, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 48, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Of course that's not totally correct, is it? In fact -- in fact, members of your brigade did -- did indeed commit or were alleged to have committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, another objection. Foundation. I haven't seen a foundation for a question like this. It is about the fifth time around that the question has been asked and General Mandic has been providing the same answer five times in a row. I think there is some sort of misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far the question is related to the Tactical Group, and there is evidence of allegations against members of the Tactical Group. There's no doubt about that. This question seems to deal with the brigade itself, the Armoured Brigade members, and the suggestion is that there are allegations against them. Now, you cannot claim that that's a repetition of an earlier question. However, the issue of foundation may arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There is -- in my submission there is foundation, and I'm getting to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please continue. We accept your assurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Defence and the Court it's 3D1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General Mandic, I don't know if you answered the question. Do you remember the question? My question was that despite what you say, members of your brigade in Kosovo were alleged to have committed serious war crimes. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Members of the 252nd Armoured Brigade committed no crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that there were allegations, reports that they had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I didn't have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Isn't that information that you would have received, members of your brigade being alleged to have committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: If members of the brigade had committed war crimes, and I'm talking about 252nd Armoured Brigade, not the Tactical Group, I would have learned through my organs from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So if -- if the brigade -- if, for example, the corps command had information that members of your brigade had committed crimes, you would have been informed of that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: If something like that happened, the corps command would probably use the regular reporting system to inform everyone. I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you don't -- you don't recall a time during your deployment in Kosovo where military security, for example, from the corps command, from the Pristina Corps command, or General Lazarevic himself ever questioning you about possible war crimes committed by your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I didn't have this sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I'm going to show you a document, and perhaps it may refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 3D1059 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, what we have here is a document from the 3rd Army security department, and you'll see that it's been sent to the Pristina Corps command, and I'll give you some time to read through; but it is essentially a report on two soldiers from your brigade, the 252nd Armoured Brigade, and I'm reading: "Having murdered with premeditation two civilians for gain namely Ismailj Bekeri and Hidajet Cena in Orahovac municipality, the municipality where, as you know, you were deployed. Does this refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do these names, the names of these soldiers, do they -- are they familiar to you at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You would agree that this is -- given the fact that it's come from the 3rd Army command and it's been sent to the Pristina Corps command, you would agree that in terms of an investigation that you should have been questioned at least. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I've never seen this before. As for the procedure in situations such as these, I'm really not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you were a brigade commander in Kosovo. You're a general. If anybody is familiar or should be familiar with these procedures, it should, I suggest, be you, and are you coming here to this court and saying that you're not aware that members of your brigade were alleged to have committed crimes and none of this means anything to you? This is nothing that you know about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: What I can say is this: I knew nothing about this, because in my brigade my security organs, battalion level, at the brigade command, and as far as I can see, I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You see the problem with this, don't you, General, that you have stated in your evidence, in your statement, that your soldiers and your unit adhered to international humanitarian law and obeyed orders in compliance with -- with the rules of international war -- law, and this report calls into question your evidence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: I can't comment on this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cepic. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid this document has not been sufficiently clarified, because there is talk here of allegations and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will be able to deal with this in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last question was argumentative, Mr. Sachdeva. Let's keep to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: You -- upon seeing this document, you must accept that members of your brigade -- I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the names on the document, including the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with many of the names of the people in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but more the active-duty component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Incidentally, General, when -- when you were involved in -- in combat activity in Orahovac, for example, and you were engaged with members of the police, the MUP, if it came to your attention that members of the MUP had committed crimes against civilians, I take it that it would have been your duty to report that to your superiors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: If I had found out that violations of international law of war had occurred, I probably would have informed my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And let me just make that clear. If you had -- or you or your fellow soldiers in the command of the brigade had learned of crimes committed by the MUP in these joint operations, combined operations, you would have reported that to your superiors. That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I had personally witnessed this, I would have reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's because in the area of combat in which your brigade was deployed, you as a member of the VJ had a legal duty to report that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, if that kind of information is obtained, it's only to be expected that this information should be passed along the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And by the same token, if members of the VJ had learnt of crimes committed by the MUP and had not reported this information up to their superiors, that would have been illegal. That would have been a violation of military duty. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that -- you say in your statement that members of the General Staff and the Supreme Staff and the Pristina Corps command visited your units during the time of your deployment. I think it was twice in May 1999. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who from the Supreme Command Staff and the Pristina Corps came to visit your units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: General Slobodan Kovacevic, chief of the armoured and mechanised units branch administration of the land forces staff of the VJ with a team of officers from the Pristina Corps. I think this occurred on or about the 10th of May. And in the second half of May, General Banjac came with an assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The officers of the Pristina Corps, do you remember who they were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zivinovic [phoen], Colonel Simic, Colonel Radovic, and I can't remember who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 27 of your statement you have given evidence about the -- the term "Joint Command," and you say in your statement that when you first received the document with the heading "Joint Command" you demanded an explanation from the corps command. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you why. Why was it that you demanded an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, the simple reason was I was only aware of the corps command, and then there was this document where the Joint Command appeared. Command implies personal responsibility, and this term "Joint Command" somehow didn't tally with my own knowledge of command. So I wanted to know why Joint Command, because that term did not tally with my notion of responsibility in relation to any tasks issued. When you say joint, that means there is a group of people performing a certain task. If you have a joint body, how can that body be made responsible for anything? There are no regulations governing that kind of situation in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who did you speak to in the Pristina Corps command about clarification of this term?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from the commander, I did not know any other officers from the Pristina Corps command. However, I knew the Chief of Operations and affairs the then-Colonel Stefanovic, Radojko quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And were you told why the term was indeed put on this document and others?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, he explained that this was a term used whenever military units were lending support to MUP units. This was a phrase, he said. And there was no Joint Command that existed, because you can't put an answer to someone who is a Joint Commander. And the only command for me in every sense was the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you -- you surely could -- surely you accept the possibility that when, as you know, there were operations involving both the MUP and the VJ that the presence of a -- of a body that was tasked in controlling and commanding those operations could exist. You agree with that? That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC
utterances.text: As far as the operations performed by my units were concerned, this body would have been too unwieldy, because all the operations, individual cases of combat, were performed at a much lower level and the involvement of the forces was very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's understood, but what I'm asking is that it's quite feasible that you would have operations on the ground, reports of those operations would be sent to the Pristina Corps commander, and from then on such reports could be sent to a Joint Command body. That's possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear a reference for that. Whoever said that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No one. This is being put as a hypothetical situation since --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let him say so then. This is a hypothesis. This is purely hypothetical. The witness should be told because this might mislead the witness and lead him to believe that actually there has been evidence to that effect. Just to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to him now from your intervention, but also the question was put on the basis "it's quite feasible that you would have operations on the ground." So that's the basis on which it's being put. Now, what's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that to all practical intents I have no answer. I knew as far as the Pristina Corps command and nothing beyond that level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point that's being put to you, though, is that you've dismissed the idea of a Joint Command because you say it's not feasible. You say -- you asked the question "How can a body be responsible for anything?" And it's being suggested to you that reporting could be done to a Joint Command body, and it could equally issue directions. Now, why do you say that's not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in order for a command to exist, it must be organised in some way, and it must have an establishment. At the head of that command there must be a person who is responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different point. I understand that entirely. But you're saying you just can't have a body that consists of a number of people which receives reports and issues directions. Now, why is that not possible? If it has its staff, why could it not be done that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never seen that body. I was never aware of the existence of that body with the exception of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's another matter as well. But you're dismissing the possibility that any such body could ever exist. Have you heard of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it able to issue directions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it able to receive reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've exhausted your time, I suspect, have you not? I thought you were going to finish tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would thus have to seek leave to continue some more tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, on what issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: More on this issue. I need to get back to the Tactical Group. I also want to discuss more on the cooperation with the MUP and one or two other minor points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We doubt very much if further exploration of this particular area is going to be productive for us. You give the impression that you need a considerable amount of time. We will allow you a further 15 minutes tomorrow, and that leaves you this evening to decide how to focus that 15 minutes. We ourselves have certain questions for the witness that will have to be dealt with also, and that would be allowing you more than probably something like 25 or 30 per cent more than would normally be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we have to terminate the proceedings for today at this stage, but there are still more questions for you to answer and they will be tomorrow. They will be in a different courtroom, Courtroom number I, and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Between now and then it's vital that you should have no communication whatsoever with any other person about the evidence in this case, and that's particularly important for you, because you're in the midst of a cross-examination. You can talk to people about whatever you wish, but you must discuss with no one any aspect of any of the evidence in this case. Could you please now leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
